headline: Anna contracts あの様な (ano yō na).
Ryōshi “should” be gyoshi: the ryō comes from confusion with 猟, which means hunting.
Na, “name”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *na; compare Okinawan nā.
Egaku is 絵 (e, “picture”) plus 書く (kaku, “write”): literally “to write a picture”.
Hikari is the nominalized stem of the verb 光る (hikaru, “to shine, to glitter, to gleam”).
Wasureru is from Old Japanese 忘る (wasuru), from Proto-Japonic *wasuru.
Jitai is 字 (“character”) plus 体 (“form”).
Shinken originally meant “real sword”, 真劍, before shifting to mean serious.
Wabiru is cognate with 侘びる (wabiru).
Zonjiru shifted from the verb 存ず (zonzu).
Juyō is from Middle Chinese 需要 (MC sju 'jiewH).
Tatoeba is the irregular -ba conditional of 例える (tatoeru, “to liken one thing to another”), attested by the Kokin Wakashū of about 920 CE.
Tsubasa is possibly a shift from 鳥 (to, “bird”) plus 総 (fusa, “tassel”), though the vowel change is irregular.
Karera is 彼 (kare) plus 等 (-ra).
Madoguchi is 窓 (mado, “window”) plus 口 (kuchi, “mouth, opening”), with kuchi voiced to guchi.
Kechi is a shift from 怪事 (keji, “unfortunate event”), and in the Edo period meant “a shabby, lowborn individual”.
Iraira is a reduplication of 刺 (ira, “thorn”).
Bōrupen is borrowed from English ball pen.
Kyanpasu is English campus, a doublet of キャンプ (kyanpu, “camp”).
Tazuneru is from Old Japanese 尋ぬ (tazunu).
Kōru is from Old Japanese 凍る (koporu), likely cognate with words for hard and stiff such as 凝る (koru, “to stiffen”).
Riku, “land”, is from Middle Chinese 陸, first attested as a standalone noun in the mid-1400s.
Kyōkasho is shortened from 教科用図書 (kyōka-yō tosho).
Sukkiri is most likely onomatopoeic; compare すきすき (sukisuki) and すきっと (sukitto), both “refreshingly”.
Kasai is from Middle Chinese 火災, and went from kwasai to kasai.
Akari originally meant natural light; the lamp sense was expressed with 灯火 (tomoshibi, literally “set alight + fire”).
Naisen is 内 (nai, “internal”) plus 線 (sen, “line”).
Hoka, “other”, may be related to Baekje ホカ (*poka, “outside”).
Sugata, “figure”, is simply from Old Japanese.
Gasorin sutando is wasei eigo (和製英語), derived from gasoline plus stand and attested from at least 1933.
Hanareru is from the Classical Japanese verb 離る (hanaru).
